Nellie Bly, the New York World's girl correspondent, feigned insanity in 1887 to get inside the asylum on Blackwell's Island, and Ten Days in a Mad-House is her report. The pamphlet's title page spells out the stunt: feigning insanity in order to reveal asylum horrors. Corset advertisements crowd the back pages, as was the custom in Munro's cheap editions.

Bly ate rotten food, bathed in ice water, and watched attendants beat the helpless, all while sane and taking notes. A grand jury freed her and backed her findings, and New York voted millions more for the asylums. The stunt invented a school of undercover reporting. Her ten days remain the founding document, plain, furious, and impossible to argue with.

Comedian Dave Smith talks hyper-inflation and fractional reserve banking with Rogan in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Smith, a libertarian comic and podcaster, is the show's regular voice on money and the state. His act is half joke, half lecture, and this segment leans lecture.

He explains how banks create money by lending, and why he thinks the system quietly taxes savers through rising prices. Rogan asks what a normal person should do with savings in such a world. The segment is a plain-language brief for the hard-money view, from a comic who treats economics as a contact sport.
